Additionally, as residents close windows to keep out smoke, with no cooling system, the building becomes uncomfortably hot. If the building has not been tested for radon, Moore Street Seniors Inc may want to consider a radon test. Radon can enter buildings connected to the ground, such as with the Moore Street Senior Apartments’ crawlspace foundation. While the crawlspace does have a vapor retarder, in high radon areas, this may not be enough to keep radon levels low. More information on radon, including how to get a local test completed, is available from the University of Alaska Fairbanks Cooperative Extension Service (https://www.uaf.edu/ces/home-environment/radon/). 10 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR) at www.nlr.gov/publications. 3.8 Envelope Considerations The building currently has triple pane windows, which are generally adequate for the Fairbanks climate as long as the seals are intact. Moore Street Seniors, Inc., has obtained State of Alaska funding to replace the windows. Considerations for replacing windows would include: • If an additional funding source can be identified, the best practice would be to replace the siding and add exterior insulation at the same time as the window replacement; this would necessitate appropriate mechanical ventilation to provide dedicated outside air since it would air-tighten the building. The funding source would need to be comprehensive to both the wall retrofit and adding mechanical ventilation. • If there is any flexibility in the funding, it may be beneficial to replace the siding and add exterior insulation in place of window replacement. This would necessitate also installing mechanical ventilation. The added insulation and reduced air leakage would help to reduce drafts and could include details around the existing windows. A detailed building energy model would help to clarify if this upgrade is cost effective. • Windows can be replaced with new triple pane windows so they remain energy efficient and do not cause a rise in energy costs for the building. • In cold climates, it is beneficial to install casement windows (hinged on one side that open like a door to the outside) with locks and hinges at more than one place on the locking side for windows that need to open. This reduces air leakage and ice formation in the winter, and egress casement windows are less likely to freeze shut than sliding windows in cold weather. Unless it is necessary for egress, double casement windows can be replaced with single casement (casement on only one side of the frame) to reduce air leakage and reduce energy costs. • If the contractor replacing the windows follows best practice cold climate building science principles ensuring to detail around the window to reduce air leakage or water intrusion, it will ensure lower energy use and costs. For instance, contractors can follow the Building Energy Efficiency Standards5, which are one example of energy efficiency practices for commercial buildings that reduce energy costs.
